title: Emotions Beat Facts in Climate Campaigns — Study
paragraphs: Climate campaigners often try to persuade people to act by presenting scientific facts and data. However, two major studies suggest that appealing to people's emotions may be far more effective.

The first study, by Mario Herberz and Tobias Brosch of the University of Geneva in Switzerland, was published in the Journal of Environmental Psychology in 2026. The researchers analyzed the results of 71 earlier studies involving a total of 216,000 participants, comparing 15 different ways of communicating about climate change. These included presenting facts, evoking emotions and highlighting the financial or health consequences of climate change.

Almost all of the strategies had some positive effect on people's intentions, behavior and support for climate policies. However, emotional approaches, such as telling stories or creating a sense of wonder at the beauty of nature, were particularly effective. Using images also made messages more effective. According to the researchers, these emotional approaches were significantly more successful than simply presenting scientific evidence. Messages based on moral or ethical ideas also performed well. In contrast, messages telling people that they had a personal or shared responsibility to act had little or no effect, and the researchers warned that they could even create mistrust.

A second study, carried out by researchers at Stanford University's Climate Cognition Lab and published in the journal PNAS Nexus, reached a similar conclusion. More than 31,000 Americans were shown one of 17 different climate messages and then offered the chance to take action, for example by signing up for newsletters, writing to politicians or donating money. Positive messages consistently worked better than negative ones. The most effective approach emphasized that collective action has worked in the past and that taking part feels good. In contrast, messages designed to make people feel guilty had no significant effect. According to Madalina Vlasceanu, the senior author of the Stanford study, many researchers had long assumed that people needed to be frightened into action. However, the study found that fear did not work for this kind of collective action.
Both studies measured people's responses to short messages, so it is not clear how well the results apply to real campaigns.
